title: IEEPA Tariff Refund Accounting: Build the Refund Register From the Books, Split Principal From Interest, and Land the Cash in the Right Entity Before Year-End
excerpt: CBP updated its IEEPA Duty Refunds page on November 2, 2026: refunds carry interest under 19 U.S.C. 1505, pay only by ACH, and arrive 60 to 90 days after a CAPE declaration is accepted, with $127.7 billion already sent to Treasury and Phase 3 open for finally liquidated entries. Here is tariff refund accounting for a multi-entity finance team: choose the loss recovery or gain contingency model once, build the refund register from the ledger, credit principal to the caption that carried the duty, book interest as other income, and move the cash to the entity that bore the cost through intercompany before year-end.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: CFO working through tariff refund accounting with a CAPE declaration list, a refund register, and a three-entity ledger open before year-end close
content:
Tariff refund accounting starts with one decision, not a journal entry: pick the loss recovery model or the gain contingency model, apply it to every IEEPA claim, post the principal back to the caption that carried the duty, and book the interest as other income. Then tie each CAPE declaration to the ledger, entity by entity.

Why this matters now

Three things changed in the last month. U.S. Customs and Border Protection's IEEPA Duty Refunds page, updated 2026-11-02, says refund interest is computed under 19 U.S.C. 1505, that every refund is paid by ACH to bank details on file in the ACE portal, and that valid refunds are generally issued within 60 to 90 days after a CAPE declaration is accepted. Money that was a contingency in the spring is now a receivable with a payment window, and it is landing in bank accounts in the middle of the fourth-quarter close.

The scale was set by the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 opinion in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, which held that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. Baker Tilly's refund tracker, updated 2026-11-01, reports CBP figures as of October 23: $137.9 billion in potential and certified refunds accepted for processing, $127.7 billion transmitted to Treasury, 3,960 Phase 3 declarations covering about 15.83 million finally liquidated entries, and $990 million in refunds delayed because the importer has no ACH details on file. Phase 3 opened on October 6 for importers that are plaintiffs at the Court of International Trade. On launch day CBP accepted 477 declarations covering 425,517 entries, per Supply Chain Dive's 2026-10-08 report. On October 8 the trade court certified a class of importers who paid IEEPA duties between February 1, 2025 and February 19, 2026, which is the only path so far for everyone with finally liquidated entries who never sued.

Audit firm and customs broker coverage explains the two accounting models and the filing mechanics. What it doesn't do is show a finance team with three entities and one importer of record how to build the refund register from the ledger, split principal from interest, and get the cash to the entity that bore the cost. That is this article.

Two models, one choice

Tariff refund accounting under US GAAP has no dedicated standard. A refund of IEEPA duties is either a recovery of a previously recognized loss, accounted for by analogy to ASC 410-30 and recognized when recovery is probable, or a gain contingency under ASC 450-30, recognized only when realized. Grant Thornton's July 22, 2026 analysis describes both as acceptable. The choice is a policy, so it applies to every claim the group holds, and it is disclosed.

QuestionLoss recovery model (ASC 410-30 by analogy)Gain contingency model (ASC 450-30)
When is the refund recognized?When recovery is probable, which many groups tie to CBP's acceptance of the CAPE declarationWhen realized: cash received, or the amount fixed with no remaining contingency
How much?Capped at the duty cost previously recognized; anything above that is a gain contingencyThe amount received
Where does the principal go?Back to the caption that carried the duty: inventory, cost of goods sold, fixed assets, or the expense lineSame captions, in the period the cash lands
Where does the interest go?Other income, when received or when fixedOther income, when received
Before recognition?Disclose the claim and the estimateDisclose the claim and the estimate
Period effectEarlier, and lumpier at acceptanceLater, and lumpier at receipt

Whichever model the group picks, presentation follows the original cost. Duty that sits in inventory still on hand reduces inventory. Duty on goods already sold reduces cost of goods sold. Duty capitalized into equipment reduces the asset's cost, and depreciation adjusts from that point forward. Duty that was expensed as a period cost reduces that line, or is shown as other income if the group prefers; Grant Thornton accepts either, applied consistently.

Polarity matters. The original duty was a debit to inventory or cost of goods sold and a credit to cash or the broker's payable. The refund is the mirror: a debit to a receivable or to cash, and a credit to the caption that carried the duty. The interest is a credit to other income, never to cost of goods sold, because no cost was ever booked for it. CBP's figures bundle the two in one ACH deposit, so the register below has to split them.

The refund register, one group's November worked through

Call the group Northline Holdings: three entities, one finance team, a December year-end. Northline Imports LLC is the importer of record and sells to Northline Retail Inc. and Northline Industrial Inc. at cost plus a margin, with the duty inside the transfer price. The figures are illustrative. Between February 2025 and February 2026 Imports paid $2.64 million of IEEPA duty on 412 entries, every dollar debited to inventory and then flowing to cost of goods sold as the goods moved to the affiliates and on to customers.

Step one: pull every IEEPA duty posting from the ledger

The register starts from the books, not from the broker's spreadsheet. The query is every posting to the duty sub-account, or to inventory with a customs broker as the vendor, dated February 2025 through February 2026, with entry number, entry date, entity, account, and amount. Northline's query returned 412 lines and $2.64 million. The broker's entry list returned 412 entries and $2.64 million. That agreement is the first tie-out, and it is the one most groups skip.

Step two: match declarations and set the model

Each CAPE declaration lists entry numbers. Northline's Phase 1 declarations, accepted in May 2026, covered 348 entries and $2.21 million of principal. Its Phase 3 declaration, accepted on October 6 because Imports had joined a trade court case in 2025, covered the remaining 64 finally liquidated entries and $430,000. Every register line now carries a declaration reference, an acceptance date, and a status. Northline chose the loss recovery model, with CBP's acceptance as the probable trigger, and wrote that policy down in May so the auditor saw it before the first cash arrived.

Step three: split principal from interest and post by caption

Between July and September, Imports received 14 ACH deposits totaling $2,293,400. CBP's liquidation notices put the principal at $2,210,000 and the interest at $83,400. At acceptance in May, under the loss recovery model, Imports had booked a receivable of $2,210,000 with the credit split by where the duty sat on that date: $190,000 of the related goods were still in Imports' inventory, so inventory took $190,000, and cost of goods sold took $2,020,000. When the cash came in, the entry was a debit to cash of $2,293,400, a credit to the receivable of $2,210,000, and a credit to interest income of $83,400. Nothing from the deposits touched cost of goods sold a second time.

Step four: land the cash in the right entity

Here is the problem that single-entity guides never reach. The refund arrived in Imports, but Imports did not bear the cost. Of the $2,020,000 credited to cost of goods sold, $1,310,000 related to goods sold on to Retail and $710,000 to goods sold on to Industrial, both at cost plus, both with the duty inside the price. On a standalone basis Retail and Industrial carried the duty in their own cost of goods sold, and the refund has made Imports look $2 million more profitable than it was.

The intercompany agreement decides what happens next. Northline's agreement says cost adjustments flow through, so Imports issued credit notes to Retail for $1,310,000 and to Industrial for $710,000 in September, reducing each affiliate's purchases and Imports' sales to affiliates. On consolidation the credit notes eliminate, and the group's cost of goods sold shows the $2,020,000 credit exactly once. The interest stayed in Imports, because Imports was the party CBP owed it to. Groups whose agreement is silent have a decision to make, and the intercompany eliminations guide covers how the pair has to be booked so it eliminates cleanly.

The margin needs protecting too. Northline's third-quarter consolidated revenue was $18.4 million against cost of goods sold of $12.9 million before the refund, a 29.9 percent gross margin. After the $2,020,000 credit the margin reads 40.9 percent. Neither the board nor the lender should see 40.9 percent without a line that says why. Northline tagged every refund posting with a class called IEEPA refund, so the board package shows margin with and without it, and the prior-year comparison stays honest.

Step five: forecast what is still outstanding

The Phase 3 declaration for $430,000 was accepted on October 6. CBP's page puts payment at 60 to 90 days after acceptance, so the cash should land between early December and early January, plus interest that CBP will calculate. Under the loss recovery model the receivable is already on the balance sheet; under the gain contingency model it is a note in the forecast and nothing in the ledger. Either way it belongs in the 13-week cash forecast as a dated inflow with a range, not a point. And the finance team checked that Imports' ACH details were on file in ACE in October, because $990 million of other importers' refunds were sitting unpaid on October 23 for exactly that reason. The 13-week cash flow forecast article covers where a dated, ranged inflow like this one goes.

Accounting controls for tariff refund accounting

Source data: the ledger postings for IEEPA duty by entity, account, entry number, and date; the broker's entry list for the same period; each CAPE declaration with its entry numbers, acceptance date, and status; CBP's liquidation or reliquidation notices showing principal and interest per entry; the ACH deposits by date and amount; the intercompany agreement; and the group's written accounting policy naming the model.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Sum the duty postings by entry and tie them to the broker's list. Match each entry to a declaration. For every accepted entry, under the loss recovery model, recognize a receivable equal to the duty previously booked and credit the caption that carried it, split by whether the related goods were on hand or sold at the acceptance date. The receivable is a point-in-time balance; the credit to cost of goods sold is a flow in the period of recognition, and it is never pushed back into the period the duty was paid. When cash arrives, clear the receivable for the principal and credit the remainder to interest income. Allocate the principal to affiliates in proportion to the duty inside the transfer prices they paid, if the agreement provides for it.

Review: a second person reruns the register from the raw ledger postings and lands on the same entry count and total; the sum of principal received plus interest received equals the ACH deposits to the cent; no deposit was credited to cost of goods sold; the receivable balance equals accepted declarations not yet paid; the intercompany credit notes equal the affiliate allocation and eliminate on consolidation; and the board package shows margin with and without the refund class.

Decision: the CFO owns the model choice and the policy memo, made once and applied to every claim. The controller owns the register and the entity allocation. The intercompany agreement, or the CFO where it is silent, decides whether affiliates share in the refund and whether interest is shared. The auditor's view on whether CBP's acceptance makes recovery probable governs the recognition date under the loss recovery model, and it is asked for in writing before the first entry is posted. The consolidated cash flow reporting article covers why a refund that lands in one entity and is shared by three needs the entity view and the group view side by side.

Limits and common mistakes

Importers that never sued and whose entries are finally liquidated have no CAPE path today. The class certified on October 8 is a route, not a refund order, and the government is widely expected to appeal. Supporting probable under the loss recovery model for those entries is hard, and most groups disclose the claim and recognize nothing until the court orders reliquidation.

Companies that paid higher prices to an importer but did not import have no refund right unless their contract gives them one. The refund belongs to the importer of record. A customer that wants a share negotiates it, and the importer books the pass-through as a price adjustment, not as a reversal of its own cost.

Interest netted into cost of goods sold overstates margin and understates other income. Principal booked to other income when the related goods are still in inventory overstates both inventory and profit. The register's on-hand versus sold column exists to prevent both.

The refund is a flow in the period it is recognized. Prior periods are not restated, and the comparison to last year will be distorted in that period. The fix is presentation, with the refund identified, not restatement.

Tax follows its own rules. A refund of duty that was deducted in an earlier year is generally income in the year it is received, and the interest is taxable interest. That is the tax adviser's call and belongs in the year-end provision, not in this register.

Northline is illustrative. CBP's timing, interest, and ACH statements are from its page updated November 2, 2026, and the October 23 figures are CBP's as reported by Baker Tilly. Both will move.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you account for an IEEPA tariff refund under US GAAP?

There is no dedicated standard. A group either treats the refund as a recovery of a previously recognized loss, by analogy to ASC 410-30, and recognizes a receivable when recovery is probable, or treats it as a gain contingency under ASC 450-30 and recognizes it only when realized. The choice is a policy applied to every claim and disclosed. Under both, the principal is credited back to the caption that carried the duty and the interest is other income.

When can a company record a tariff refund receivable?

Only under the loss recovery model, and only when recovery is probable. Many groups treat CBP's acceptance of the CAPE declaration as that point, since CBP states that valid refunds are generally issued within 60 to 90 days after acceptance. The auditor's view governs. Under the gain contingency model nothing is recorded until the cash is received or the amount is fixed with no remaining contingency.

Where does the interest on a tariff refund go?

Other income, in the period it is received or fixed. CBP calculates interest under 19 U.S.C. 1505 and pays it in the same ACH deposit as the principal, so the deposit has to be split using CBP's liquidation notice. Crediting the whole deposit to cost of goods sold overstates gross margin.

What if our entity was not a plaintiff and the entries are finally liquidated?

CAPE Phase 3 is limited to importers that are plaintiffs at the Court of International Trade with court-ordered reliquidation. The court certified a class of importers who paid IEEPA duties between February 1, 2025 and February 19, 2026 on October 8, 2026, but certification is not a refund order and an appeal is expected. Most groups disclose the claim and recognize nothing for those entries until the court orders reliquidation.

Does a tariff refund go to cost of goods sold or other income?

It goes where the duty went. Duty on goods already sold comes back through cost of goods sold. Duty on goods still in inventory reduces inventory. Duty capitalized into equipment reduces the asset's cost. Duty expensed as a period cost may reduce that line or be shown as other income, applied consistently. Interest is always other income.

Once the register is built from the ledger rather than from the broker's list, the refund stops being a surprise in one entity's income statement and becomes a dated receivable the whole group can see. FinBoard reads every entity's QuickBooks file into one consolidated view, so a finance team can see the duty postings, the refund credits, and the intercompany pair by entity on one page, drill from any total to the entries behind it, and show the board margin with and without the refund. See how FinBoard puts every entity's refund postings on one page.
